chunks: I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the bequest for the inheritor, so he said: 'Permissible.'

key_terms.الْوَارِثُ: warith — the legal inheritor; one who receives a fixed share of the estate (farida) according to Islamic inheritance law
key_terms.الْوَصِيَّةُ: wasiyya — a testamentary bequest; a legal instruction given before death to distribute part of one's estate (up to one-third) to designated recipients
key_terms.تَجُوزُ: tajuz — it is permissible; a standard jurisprudential verdict indicating legal validity, from the root j-w-z meaning to pass or be allowed

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible in Shia Islam to make a bequest (wasiyya) for one's legal inheritors?
ai.summary: Muhammad ibn Muslim asked Imam al-Sadiq (AS) whether it is permissible to make a bequest (wasiyya) in favor of one's legal inheritors. The Imam's terse one-word answer, 'Permissible,' confirms that leaving a bequest to an heir in addition to their share of inheritance is legally valid in Shia jurisprudence. This ruling addressed a live debate in early Islamic jurisprudence, where some scholars held that a bequest to an inheritor conflicted with the Quranic inheritance system of fixed shares.
